This study – which evaluates the load response of various end-use devices to hourly dynamic prices – is particularly timely, given that the State’s Load Management Standards (LMS) require all of California’s large utilities and community choice aggregators (CCA) to provide dynamic electricity pricing options to customers by 2027. By modeling possible dispatch algorithms and assessing the resulting impacts on both individual bills and the overall grid, the California Price Response Potential Study provides policy-relevant information on the potential benefits and challenges associated with dynamic pricing, as well as considerations for the design of dynamic pricing tariffs. Additionally, this study explores the cost-effectiveness of adopting automation technologies to enable devices to respond more effectively to real-time price signals, thereby moving away from the greater emphasis on manual responses considered in previous efforts. This exploration takes into account a range of price profiles – which allow for differences across utilities and customer classes – and scenarios in which the percentage of total costs that are allocated dynamically (versus fixed portions of the hourly volumetric price) vary. Most results presented focus on 2030. 4 1.2 Policy context California has been progressing efforts towards dynamic prices for nearly a decade. Appendix A provides a detailed documentation of the policies and actions that have been enacted in the state before and during the completion of this study. These policies are summarized in Table 1. This study aims to inform these efforts by describing the potential load response and bill savings impacts of automated end use response to dynamic prices, and the impact that various price levels and designs have on those outcomes.
